revisions.title: Socrates’ portrait of verbal combat
revisions.body: Socrates presents the brothers’ eristic as a kind of verbal combat: they are said to refute whatever is said alike whether false or true. The point is not yet that this skill has been demonstrated; it is the unsettling portrait Socrates offers Crito, in which success in argument is detached from the truth of the claim.

revisions.title: The victory that leaves no room for correction
revisions.body: Try hearing this passage not as a proof but as a trap for the proof-maker. Socrates lets the brothers’ rule expand until false belief, ignorance, and even refutation lose their place. My reading is that the comedy comes from this mismatch: a doctrine claiming total victory also removes the shared conditions that make correction—and therefore any serious exchange—possible.

revisions.title: When praise joins the joke
revisions.body: The applause is not allowed to settle the scene. Socrates first joins it, praising the pair in a voice so lavish that the compliment becomes part of the joke. My reading is that the praise works as a trap: it lets the audience enjoy the display while making us hear how little separates admiration from ridicule. The scene therefore turns public delight into a question about what, exactly, the crowd is applauding.

body: "Applause supplies the surface; Socrates' mock praise supplies the twist. He does not say that the arguments refute their own speakers. He imagines instead that most people would be ashamed to use them for refuting others. Then the closing advice turns compliment into warning: a trick learned instantly loses prestige, so its champions should keep it private—and charge for access. The praise begins to sound like an exposure of scarcity masquerading as excellence."
